query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal aging across service-regime temperatures induces a kinetic pathway in the Mg-containing lightweight HEA where Mg segregates to precipitate/matrix interfaces, triggering the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds. This process depletes the matrix of Mg necessary for forming a protective oxide scale, thereby impairing the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance compared to the initial metastable solid-solution state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution in a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with homogeneous Mg distribution and minimal intermetallic phase formation.
generation.intervention: Controlled isothermal aging at service-relevant temperatures (spanning moderate to high regimes) for varied durations.
generation.conditions: Comparison between samples maintained at baseline conditions (low temperature/short aging time) and samples exposed to elevated temperatures over longer durations, using in-situ synchrotron XRD and high-resolution TEM, supplemented by STEM-EDS to track local Mg partitioning.
generation.structural_mediator: The growth of Mg-partitioned intermetallic phases at precipitate/matrix boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation enhances diffusion leading to Mg segregation at interfaces, which in turn nucleates intermetallic precipitates. This transformation reduces the available Mg for forming a protective Mg-rich oxide layer, thus undermining both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will exhibit increased intermetallic phase volume fractions and localized Mg depletion in the matrix. These microstructural changes will correlate with a measurable decline in corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the unaged, homogeneous metastable state.
generation.baseline: The unaged, metastable state with a uniform Mg distribution and high corrosion/oxidation resistance.
generation.boundary: Service conditions defined by a lower temperature/short duration regime (preserving the metastable state) versus a higher temperature/prolonged aging regime (promoting intermetallic formation and performance degradation).
generation.uncertainty: The specific aging temperature thresholds and kinetics of Mg segregation and intermetallic precipitation are not precisely known and may vary with subtle changes in composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject a set of Mg-containing HEA samples to isothermal aging at a series of temperatures spanning from baseline (e.g., room temperature or modest service temperature) to elevated service-relevant temperatures for controlled durations. Compare these with unaged control samples using in-situ synchrotron XRD to detect phase changes, high-resolution TEM to image intermetallic precipitates, and STEM-EDS mapping to assess Mg distribution.
measurements: Phase identification and quantification using synchrotron XRD
Microstructural imaging and precipitate detection via high-resolution TEM
Elemental mapping of Mg segregation using STEM-EDS
Corrosion rate measurements and high-temperature oxidation resistance tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not lead to significant Mg segregation and intermetallic phase formation, or if the protective oxide scale and associated corrosion/oxidation resistances remain unchanged from the baseline state under service-relevant conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, we developed a low-density (2.4 g/cm3) and high specific yield strength (344 × 103 N·m/kg) Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 CCA with a single-phase face-centered cubic (SP-FCC) structure by applying high pressure and high temperature (HPHT) to promote the transition from IMCs to solid solutions. The formation of the SP-FCC lattice is attributed to the decreased differences in atomic size and electronegativity between the solute elements and Al under high pressure, as well as the synergistic high entropy effect caused by high temperature and high pressure. The distinct solid solution strengthening comes from the incorporation of multiple elements in one single FCC lattice, as well as the significant pinning effect of dislocations from nanoscale chemical fluctuations, which leads to the enhanced strength of the low-density CCA.

cited_evidence.text: As observed during the isothermal oxidation process, the outer oxide layers of the FeNiCuAlCo and FeNiCuAlMn HEAs develop wrinkles, while the inner oxide layers bend and may even detach from the substrate (Figure 7b,c), leading to the formation of an irregular oxide layer. In contrast, the oxide film of the FeNiCuAlCr HEA is denser and remains free of cracks. Figure 8 is a schematic of the oxidation mechanism of FeNiCuAlCr alloys in air at 900 °C. In the oxidation process of FeNiCuAlCr high-entropy alloys, Al2O3 initially forms on the surface, where it acts as a passivating layer, preventing further oxygen diffusion and thereby limiting the oxidation of internal elements. Subsequently, chromium oxide and copper oxide layers form. As the oxidation progresses, the Al2O3 and Cr2O3 oxide layers grow thicker and merge, with oxygen gradually migrating inward. Over time, under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the system reaches local equilibrium in oxygen partial pressure, leading to the formation of continuous spinel-type oxides (NiFe2O4) due to reactions between Ni and Fe oxides. These factors contribute to the excellent high-temperature oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAlCr alloys.
